'Li Xiaogong was able to persuade the Sui cities in modern southern Shaanxi, Sichuan, and Chongqing to submit' (Emperor Gaozu page, in the paragraph on the winter-617 capture of Chang'an, before Emperor Yang's death in spring 618); the Li Xiaogong page: Li Yuan 'made Li Xiaogong in charge of a campaign to persuade or capture the region south of the Qinling Mountains' and 'Li Xiaogong was able to persuade some 30 commanderies to submit to Li Yuan'. Neither page gives a month or year; the event is placed at the proclamation (month 6 is a placement, not a page date) because the state begins then. [fx-11, 2026-11-01] Added for the 623 snap: Cliopatria's 623 outline holds 1,247 Sichuan and 103 Chongqing cells that no ledger event had given the Tang.

region.text: 'much of the territory in modern eastern Gansu' (the page), as radii round Lanzhou and Tianshui

ledger.note: Dec 618: Li Shimin destroys Xue Rengao's Qin. The Transition page: Xue Ju 'died in early 618 and was succeeded by his son Xue Rengao'; Li Shimin 'defeated and killed Xue Rengao, annexing his Qin state into Tang' (no month). The Xue Ju page dates Xue Ju's death to 3 September 618 and says Xue Rengao 'was defeated by and forced to surrender to Li Shimin three months later' (its Qinxing era ends 30 November 618), so the annexation is placed in December 618, after the Tang's proclamation, as the xue-ju-s-qin dossier does (618-12). [fx-11, 2026-11-01] Region widened from the Tianshui disc alone to the founding region of the xue-ju-s-qin dossier (Lanzhou 100 km plus Tianshui 150 km: the Xue Ju page's Qin land in Gansu), so the two dossiers mirror each other; Cliopatria's 623 Tang outline holds Gansu cells the ledger did not give the Tang.

region.text: Wuwei, Zhangye, Dunhuang, Xiping (Xining) and Fuhan (Linxia): the land west of the Yellow River

ledger.note: 619: Li Gui's state surrenders to the Tang. 'Around the same time, Li Gui's official An Xinggui captured Li Gui in a coup and surrendered the state to Tang' (the paragraph after 'In summer 619, Wang Shichong had Yang Tong yield the throne to him'). [fx-11, 2026-11-01] Region widened from the Hexi Corridor alone to the land of the li-gui-s-liang dossier (the Hexi Corridor plus Xining and Linxia, 60 km each: Wuwei, Zhangye, Dunhuang, Xiping and Fuhan), so the two dossiers mirror each other; the Emperor Gaozu page confirms the surrender: 'Gaozu executed Li Gui and incorporated his domain into Tang' (summer 619).

region.text: Taiyuan and its plain, where Liu Wuzhou moved his capital in 619 (Liu Wuzhou dossier); the Transition page says only that he took 'much of modern Shanxi'

ledger.note: 619: Liu Wuzhou takes Shanxi from the Tang. 'Liu Wuzhou made a major attack south, taking over much of modern Shanxi, which Tang had controlled' (Transition page, around 619); 'In late 619, Tang forces, commanded by Li Shimin, began a counterattack'. The page names no city or month; Taiyuan, Li Yuan's old base, is the researcher's reading.

region.text: Liu Wuzhou's Dingyang state, 'taking over much of modern Shanxi' (619) and 'His Dingyang state was integrated into Tang' (summer 620); the page names no town, so the region is Shanxi

ledger.note: 620: Liu Wuzhou's Dingyang annexed. 'In late 619, Tang forces, commanded by Li Shimin, began a counterattack against Liu Wuzhou'; 'By summer 620, Li Shimin had defeated Liu, who abandoned his territory and fled to Eastern Goktürk'; 'His Dingyang state was integrated into Tang.' [fx-11, 2026-11-01] Region changed from the Taiyuan (100 km) and Datong (200 km) circles to Shanxi, the province the Transition page names ('taking over much of modern Shanxi, which Tang had controlled'); the Datong circle ran 223 cells into Inner Mongolia and 191 into Hebei, where nothing opened puts Liu Wuzhou's state.

region.text: Gao Kaidao's Yan, in northern Hebei (Cliopatria row 623-625; the page gives no boundary)

ledger.note: 620: Gao Kaidao submits to the Tang. 'In 620, he briefly submitted to Emperor Gaozu of Tang and was bestowed the imperial surname of Li'; in winter 620 Gaozu created him Prince of Beiping and commissioned him commandant at Wei Prefecture. A vassal tint, rule 4.

region.text: Du Fuwei's land 'south of the Huai River': Anhui and Jiangsu south of 33.3 N (the polygon is an approximation of the river line); without Piling (Changzhou), which Li Zitong took from Shen Faxing in 620 and held until winter 621

ledger.note: 620: Du Fuwei's land is the Tang's. 'In summer 620, Emperor Gaozu changed Du Fuwei's title to Prince of Wu, and bestowed on him the imperial surname of Li' (Du Fuwei page, which has him decide to submit in 619; the Emperor Gaozu page: 'the rebel leader Du Fuwei, who controlled the modern southern Anhui, submitted to Tang', summer 619; the Transition page, 619 paragraph: 'Du Fuwei, who submitted to Tang and was created the Prince of Wu'). The Du Fuwei page gives his state as the land south of the Huai River, at Liyang (Chaohu, Anhui) and from 620 at Danyang (Nanjing); he died in April 624 and Fu Gongshi's Song (624 event below) takes over part of it. Mirror of the du-fuwei-s-regime dossier (dissolve 620, Nanjing circle of 130 km), with a wider region because the page names the whole land south of the Huai. [fx-11, 2026-11-01] Added for the 623 snap: Cliopatria's 623 outline holds Anhui and Jiangsu cells that no ledger event had given the Tang. [fx-11 review, 2026-11-01] Changzhou (80 km, the circle of the li-zitong-s-wu dossier) taken out of this gain: the Du Fuwei page has Li Zitong take Piling (Changzhou) and Zhejiang from Shen Faxing in 620 and surrender only in winter 621, when Li Fuwei 'controlled all of the territory south of the Huai River'; the 621 gain of Li Zitong's Wu brings the circle to the Tang.

region.text: Gao Kaidao's Yan

ledger.note: 621: Gao Kaidao rebels against the Tang. 'in 621 he rebelled against Tang and reasserted independence'; in winter 621 he kept the supplies Li Yi sent, 'breaking off the relations with Li Yi and the Tang dynasty'; he allied with the Eastern Turks and Liu Heita.

region.text: Wang Shichong's Zheng, capital Luoyang (summer 619: 'establishing a new state of Zheng'); 'In fear, Wang surrendered' at Hulao

ledger.note: 621: Wang Shichong's Zheng annexed. After Hulao (spring 621) 'Wang's Zheng state and Dou's Xia state were annexed by Tang'; Li Shimin had put the Zheng capital Luoyang under siege. The page gives no month for Wang's surrender.

region.text: Xiao Xian's Liang, capital Jiangling: 'most of his state was annexed by Tang' (Transition page); the state 'included most of modern Hubei, Hunan, Guangxi, and northern Vietnam' (Xiao Xian page); the Transition page names only Jiangling

ledger.note: 621: Xiao Xian surrenders at Jiangling. 'Also in 621, Emperor Gaozu's nephew Li Xiaogong the Prince of Zhao Commandery attacked Xiao Xian's Liang state', put Jiangling under siege, and Xiao 'surrendered'; 'most of his state was annexed by Tang'. The Xiao Xian page gives the state as most of Hubei, Hunan, Guangxi and northern Vietnam, so the gain is widened from the Jiangling area to the whole state, as the xiao-xian-s-liang dissolve is.

region.text: Li Zitong's Wu, which 'controlled Jiangdu and the surrounding regions' (Transition page), with the territory he took from Shen Faxing in 620, 'roughly modern Zhejiang', capital Piling (Changzhou) (Li Zitong page)

ledger.note: 621: Li Zitong's Wu annexed. 'Around the same time, Li Fuwei defeated Li Zitong, forcing Li Zitong's surrender, and Li Zitong's Wu state was also annexed by Tang' (Transition page; the sentence gives no year); the Li Zitong page has his defeat at Hangzhou in winter 621 and his 620 conquest of Shen Faxing's land, 'roughly modern Zhejiang', so the gain covers Zhejiang as well as Jiangdu (Yangzhou).

region.text: the Shandong land 'controlled by the agrarian leader Xu Yuanlang but had successively submitted to Zheng and then to Tang'

ledger.note: 621: Shandong passes to the Tang. The Transition page, in its 621 paragraph (which opens with Li Shimin's advance to Hulao Pass), has the land 'which had been controlled by the agrarian leader Xu Yuanlang but had successively submitted to Zheng and then to Tang'. Mirror of the xu-yuanlang-s-lu dossier (ledger 1, 621: Xu submits to the Tang). The page names no town, so the region is the Shandong region (the researcher's reading of 'Shandong'). [fx-11, 2026-11-01] Added for the 623 snap: Cliopatria's 623 outline holds 693 Shandong cells that no ledger event had given the Tang.

region.text: Dongping (modern Heze), Yan Prefecture (modern Jining) and Langye (modern Linyi): the three circles of the xu-yuanlang-s-lu dossier

ledger.note: 621: Xu Yuanlang rises against the Tang. The Transition page, 621 section: Xu 'rose as well' and 'declared himself the Prince of Lu' (no month); the Emperor Gaozu page: 'Xu Yuanlang, a rebel leader who had previously submitted to Zheng, also rose in revolt, occupying the modern Shandong region'. Only the three circles of the xu-yuanlang-s-lu dossier leave the Tang here, because the pages name no other town. Mirror of xu-yuanlang-s-lu ledger 2. [fx-11, 2026-11-01]

region.text: Dou Jiande's Xia, after the Battle of Hulao: 'Wang's Zheng state and Dou's Xia state were annexed by Tang' (Transition page)

ledger.note: 621: Li Shimin wins at Hulao and Dou Jiande's Xia is annexed. 'he defeated Dou Jiande (573-621) at Luoyang in the Battle of Hulao on May 28, 621' (Tang page); the Transition page: 'In spring 621 ... Li Shimin advanced east to the important Hulao Pass', captured Dou, and Xia was annexed. The page gives the cities, not a boundary; Hebei is the researcher's reading of Xia.

region.text: 'the former Xia territory', reoccupied by Liu Heita

ledger.note: 622: Liu Heita retakes the former Xia land. 'In spring 622, Li Shimin defeated Liu Heita, forcing Liu to flee to the Eastern Goktürks'; 'Liu returned later that year with Eastern Goktürk aid, reoccupying the former Xia territory'.

region.text: Lin Shihong's Chu: he 'controlled most of modern Jiangxi and Guangdong' (Lin Shihong page)

ledger.note: 622: Lin Shihong's Chu ends and passes to the Tang. 'In fear, in winter 622, Lin offered to surrender to Tang, but soon regretted it'; 'He died in 622, and his followers scattered', 'ending his state of Chu', and the page lists the Tang emperor as his successor. The Transition page: 'Earlier, Lin Shihong had died, and his Chu state dissipated, with the cities gradually submitting to Tang' (before spring 623). The year is the pages'; the exact land that passed is the researcher's reading (Jiangxi and Guangdong).

region.text: the former Xia territory

ledger.note: 623: Liu Heita is betrayed and executed. 'in spring 623, Liu, in flight, was betrayed by his official Zhuge Dewei and executed by Li Jiancheng'; the former Xia land returns to the Tang.

region.text: Dongping (modern Heze), Yan Prefecture (modern Jining) and Langye (modern Linyi): the three circles of the xu-yuanlang-s-lu dossier

ledger.note: 623: Xu Yuanlang is killed and the Tang take back his land. The Transition page, after Liu Heita's execution in spring 623: 'Xu, who had repeatedly been defeated by Tang forces, was also killed in flight'; the Xu Shiji page has him abandon his capital at Yan Prefecture by spring 623 and die in flight. Mirror of the xu-yuanlang-s-lu dossier (contest end and dissolve, 623). [fx-11, 2026-11-01]

region.text: Fu Gongshi's Song state at Danyang, 'the territory formerly under Li Fuwei's control'

ledger.note: 624: Fu Gongshi's Song crushed. Fu 'rebelled at Danyang, declaring himself the Emperor of Song'; 'By 624, Li Xiaogong had defeated and killed Fu, reintegrating Song territory into Tang'.

region.text: Gao Kaidao's Yan state in extreme northern Hebei: 'his Yan state was also integrated into Tang'

ledger.note: 624: Gao Kaidao's Yan passes to the Tang. 'By 624 ... Gao, faced with a coup led by his subordinate Zhang Jinshu, committed suicide, and his Yan state was also integrated into Tang' (Transition page); the Gao Kaidao page: Zhang Jinshu 'surrendering to Tang'. Cliopatria's Gao Kaidao row runs one year longer (625).

region.text: the Ordos, Liang Shidu's territory

ledger.note: 628: the last warlord falls. 'Civil war in China was almost totally diminished by 626, along with the 628 defeat of the Ordos warlord Liang Shidu.'

region.text: areas of the Ordos Desert and the Eastern Turkic lands south of the Gobi

ledger.note: 630: the Eastern Turks fall. 'The Tang dynasty overthrew the Eastern Turkic Khaganate in 630' and 'Illig was captured in 630' (Eastern Turkic page; infobox 'Conquest by Tang dynasty: 630'); the Tang page: 'In 630, Tang armies captured areas of the Ordos Desert'. The Eastern Turkic page's 629 attack: 'Six Tang armies attacked on a 1,200 km (750 mi) front'. The page gives no month for Illig's capture.

region.text: the Ashina settled inside the Ordos Loop, then between the Yellow River and the Gobi

ledger.note: 630-645: the Turks as Tang vassals. Infobox 'Vassal khaganate of the Tang dynasty (630–639)' and 'Buffer state of the Tang dynasty (639–645)'; 'Taizong made the Ashina live inside the Ordos Loop'; driven south of the river by the Xueyantuo in 642; 'Reconquest by Tang dynasty: 645'.

region.text: the Tuyuhun around Qinghai Lake

ledger.note: 634: the Tuyuhun become a Tang vassal (infobox 'Vassal of the Tang dynasty: 634'). The Tang page records 'separate campaigns against the Tuyuhun' under Taizong without a date. The tuyuhun dossier (ea-03) records a Tang-Tuyuhun war in 634-635 before Murong Nuohebo's vassal reign (635-672 on the Tuyuhun page); the infobox year 634 is used.

region.text: Gaochang (Turpan), made Xi Prefecture, seat of the Anxi Protectorate from 11 October 640

ledger.note: 640: Gaochang conquered; the Anxi protectorate founded. 'On 19 September 640 Hou Junji of Tang conquered Gaochang and set up Xi Prefecture in its place'; 'Xi Prefecture became the seat of the Anxi Protectorate on 11 October.' Cliopatria has no Gaochang polity.

region.text: Karasahr (Yanqi), conquered in 644; Aksu garrisoned

ledger.note: 644: Karasahr taken. 'By 644 Karasahr was also conquered, and was known to the Chinese as Yanqi' (Anxi page). The Western Turks page lists the campaigns 'against Gaochang in 640, Karasahr in 644 and 648' and a second campaign in 648 under Ashina She'er.

region.text: the Ashina buffer state between the Yellow River and the Gobi

ledger.note: 645: the buffer khaganate ends with the Tang reconquest (infobox 'Reconquest by Tang dynasty: 645'); Chebi Khan's revival attempt (646-650) fails. Cliopatria ends its Eastern Göktürks row in 632.

region.text: the Xueyantuo khaganate, 'from the Altai Mountains to the Gobi Desert': northern Mongolia

ledger.note: 1 August 646: the Tang and the Uyghurs destroy the Xueyantuo. 'On August 1, 646, the Xueyantuo were defeated by the Uyghurs (Huihe) and the Tang'; the Tang then organise the Tiele and Uyghur tribes of the plain into the Yanran protectorate (647, next events), which the keyframes draw as vassal tint. The Xueyantuo page does not say what the Tang took; the Pacify the North page ties the 647 surrender to 'the Xueyantuo's conquest in 646'.

region.text: from Lake Baikal to the north, the Gobi Desert to the south, the Greater Khingan to the east and the Altai Mountains to the west: the former Xueyantuo territory

ledger.note: 647: the steppe submits; the Yanran protectorate founded. Thirteen Tiele and Uyghur tribes surrender on 9 January 647 and are organised into 'six commanderies and seven tributary prefectures under the Jimi system'; the Yanran Protectorate, created 10 April 647, 'controlled the Mongolian Plateau from 647 to 682'. Indirect rule: vassal tint (rule 4), not the direct colour Cliopatria draws from 633. The Anbei page links the surrender to 'the Xueyantuo's conquest in 646' (the xueyantuo dossier, ea-03, ends in 646 with the Tang as successor).

region.text: Kucha, the new seat of Anxi, and the Four Garrisons: Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar, Karasahr

ledger.note: 648: Kucha falls; the Four Garrisons. 'In 648, the Tang conquered Kucha, known to the Chinese as Qiuci' (Anxi page); 'The Four Garrisons ... were installed between 648 and 658 as garrisons under the western protectorate'. The Western Turks page has the second Karasahr campaign under Ashina She'er in 648 and 'Kucha surrendered on 19 January 649'.

region.text: Kucha, known to the Chinese as Qiuci

ledger.note: 648: Kucha conquered. 'In 648, the Tang conquered Kucha, known to the Chinese as Qiuci' (Anxi page; the Western Turks page has its surrender on 19 January 649).

region.text: the Western Turkic Khaganate's lands north of the Tianshan and in the Chu and Ili valleys (Suyab), after Su Dingfang's victory on the Irtysh

ledger.note: 657: the Western Turks fall; the Tang at its largest. 'the khaganate was annexed after General Su Dingfang defeated Qaghan Ashina Helu in 657' and 'By the end of the 657 campaign, the Tang had reached its largest extent' (Western Turks page). The page names the Tarim Basin, Xinjiang, the Altai Mountains, Kyrgyzstan and Tashkent and does not mention Dzungaria, Semirechye, Sogdia or Tokharistan: the region is the researcher's reading (confidence 2). The Anxi page: 'In 658 the seat was moved back to Qiuci after Su Dingfang defeated the Western Turkic Khaganate'. The Turgesh take Suiye (Suyab) in 719 (ledger loss).

region.text: the kingdom of Baekje, 'toppled in 660 by a Tang–Silla invasion'

ledger.note: 660: Baekje destroyed. 'their kingdom was toppled in 660 by a Tang-Silla invasion' (Tang page). Tang commanderies held the land until 'In 671, Silla drove Tang forces out of most of Baekje's former territory' (Silla-Tang page).

region.text: Sogdia and Tokharistan, where the Tang had 'influence in Transoxiana' rather than rule

ledger.note: 661: the lands west of the Pamirs as Tang clients. The year is Cliopatria's (its 661-665 shape reaches 58 E), not a page's; the Talas page says the 751 defeat 'marked the end of Tang influence in Transoxiana', so influence existed. A gap-filler should open 'Protectorate General to Pacify the West' sections on the sixteen jimi protectorates of 661, or the Wikipedia article on Tokharistan.

region.text: the Azha or Tuyuhun kingdom, 'defeated by the Tibetan army and gradually assimilated into Tibetan culture'

ledger.note: 663: the Tuyuhun fall to Tibet (tibetan-empire takes the land). 'In 663, the Azha or Tuyuhun kingdom, which had served as a buffer between Tibet and China' was defeated by the Tibetan army (Tibetan Empire page, which also says 'In 635-36, the Emperor attacked and defeated the Tuyuhun'). The Tuyuhun page's infobox gives 'Destroyed by the Tibetan Empire: 670' instead and Cliopatria ends the row in 665; the 663 of the Tibetan page is used. The ruling house migrated east under Murong Nuohebo (Tuyuhun page).

region.text: Zhetysu and the Chu valley with Chach, the Nushibi and Duolu tribes under the Tang puppet qaghans

ledger.note: 666: the Western Turks under Tang overlordship (mirror of turks /ledger/1). Western Turkic Khaganate page infobox: 'Vassal of the Tang dynasty (657–742)', with the Kunling Protectorate (657–736) and the Mengchi Protectorate (657–742); Protectorate General to Pacify the West page: in 658 the office was given authority over the former Western Turkic lands, 'then split into the Mengchi and Kunling protectorates'; the page lists Ashina Mishe (657–662) and Ashina Buzhen (657–667) among the protectorate claimants and says 'After this there were several puppet khagans.' The relation begins in 657-658, before the turks dossier's first year, so 666 is that state's start (confidence 2); the pages do not say which tribes either protectorate covered. The Tang hold is overlordship over the Zhetysu and Chu lands, which the Tang keyframes of 666-681 leave to the turks dossier. [fx-35, from a membership-B handoff]

region.text: Goguryeo's territory in Manchuria and the northern Korean Peninsula, 'divided into 9 commanderies, 42 prefectures, and 100 counties' under the Protectorate General to Pacify the East at Pyongyang

ledger.note: 668: Goguryeo destroyed; the Protectorate General to Pacify the East at Pyongyang. 'After the Goguryeo-Tang War ended in 668, the Korean kingdoms of Baekje and Goguryeo were occupied'; 'Emperor Gaozong of Tang created the office of Protectorate General to Pacify the East to administer the conquered territories ... The protectorate was based in Pyongyang' (Silla-Tang page); the Tang page: 'the Kingdom of Goguryeo was destroyed by 668'. Goguryeo revolted from 669. The land is not held to 907: the ledger takes Hwanghae and the south of the Taedong in 676 (Silla), the Pyongyang district in 682, Manchuria east of Liaodong in 705 and Liaodong in 714, the last three at confidence 1 (the pages date the Andong seat's moves, not the losses).

region.text: all of the Chinese Four Garrisons of Anxi in the Tarim Basin; the seat withdrawn to Suyab

ledger.note: 670: the Four Garrisons fall to Tibet. 'In 670 the Tibetan Empire routed a Tang army at the Battle of Dafei River and attacked Gumo as well as captured Qiuci' (Anxi page; the seat moved to Suyab); the Tibetan Empire page: 'In the spring of 670, Tibet attacked the remaining Chinese territories in the western Tarim Basin'. Cliopatria keeps the Tarim in the Tang shape until 673 (its 674-681 shape lacks the Tarim, the Turpan basin and Beiting).

region.text: former Baekje and the Goguryeo lands south of the Taedong River

ledger.note: 670: the Silla-Tang War begins. Infobox dates: '670-676' (the lead: 'from 668 to 676'). The page records Goguryeo uprisings every year 669-673 and that 'In 671, Silla drove Tang forces out of most of Baekje's former territory'; the first ground change the page dates is 671.

region.text: 'In 671, Silla drove Tang forces out of most of Baekje's former territory'

ledger.note: 671: Silla drives the Tang out of most of Baekje. 'In 671, Silla drove Tang forces out of most of Baekje's former territory.'

region.text: Qiuci and the Western Regions

ledger.note: 673: the Tang retake Qiuci. 'The Tang also captured Qiuci and established control over the Western Regions in the same year' (the sentence follows a 673 entry; the page gives no 674 or 675 entry).

region.text: the Duolu country in Dzungaria, east of the Chu

ledger.note: 674: the Dzungaria piece enters the same Tang overlordship (mirror of turks /ledger/3). Protectorate General to Pacify the West page: 'In 673 the Tang consolidated control over the Wuduolu Turks living in the area that came to be known as Dzungaria'; the year is Cliopatria's 674 (the turks dossier) against the page's 673. [fx-35]

region.text: the territory south of the Taedong River

ledger.note: 676: the war ends in Silla's favour. 'In 676, Silla took all the territory south of the Taedong River in a series of battles that ended with a Silla victory at Gibeolpo in November'; Maeso, September 675: Li Jinxing's 200,000 were 'defeated' (the page notes a dissenting reading). The Andong seat moved to Liaoyang (the footnote's 676 'Old City of Liaodong'), then Xincheng in 677.

region.text: the rest of the territory south of the Taedong River (Baekje had gone in 671): 'Silla recaptured the territory south of Taedong River, while Tang held control over former Goguryeo territory north of Taedong River'

ledger.note: 676: Korea south of the Taedong passes to Silla. Infobox result: 'Silla victory'; 'Silla recaptured the territory south of Taedong River, while Tang held control over former Goguryeo territory north of Taedong River'. 'Silla failed to regain the former Goguryeo territories north of the Taedong River, which were now under Tang dominion.' Cliopatria's Silla row ends 681 and Unified Silla begins 682, so the Silla dossiers should show the land from 671 and 676.

region.text: Zhetysu and the Chu valley with Chach

ledger.note: 677: Duzhi's rebellion ends the Tang overlordship over the Chu and Zhetysu lands (mirror of turks /ledger/4). Protectorate General to Pacify the West page: in 677 Ashina Duzhi, 'previously a Tang general tasked with controlling the Wuduolu Turks', rebelled and proclaimed himself ruler of all Turks, taking the title Onoq Khagan; the Western Turkic Khaganate page lists Ashina Duzhi (676–679), allied with the Tibetan Empire; in 679 'the Tang general, Pei Xingjian, defeated Ashina Duzhi' (Protectorate page). That the declaration ends the overlordship is the turks dossier's reading (confidence 2). [fx-35]

region.text: the Duolu country in Dzungaria, east of the Chu

ledger.note: 677: the Dzungaria piece leaves the Tang overlordship with Duzhi's declaration: his own tribes are the Wuduolu Turks of Dzungaria whom the Tang had assigned to him (mirror of turks /ledger/5). Same page and reading as the entry above. [fx-35]

region.text: Qiuci (Kucha)

ledger.note: 677: Tibet takes Qiuci again. 'In 677 the Tibetan Empire captured Qiuci'; in the same year Ashina Duzhi, a Tang general, rebelled and declared himself Onoq Khagan.

region.text: the Four Garrisons, control re-established by Pei Xingjian

ledger.note: 679: the Tarim recovered. 'In 679 the Tang general, Pei Xingjian, defeated Ashina Duzhi as well as the Tibetans' and 'established control over the Western Regions' (Anxi page). The same page: 'The Tang also captured Qiuci and established control over the Western Regions in the same year' (673, the year of the sentence before) and 'In 677 the Tibetan Empire captured Qiuci'.

region.text: the plateau the Yanran/Anbei protectorate 'controlled from 647 to 682'

ledger.note: 682: the steppe is lost to the Second Turkic Khaganate ('Second Turkic Khaganate established: 682', Eastern Turkic page). The Anbei page: 'It controlled the Mongolian Plateau from 647 to 682'; 'In 683, Ilterish Qaghan besieged the Chanyu Protectorate'; 'In 686, the status of the Chanyu Protectorate was downgraded to zhenshou shi'. Cliopatria's 'Turgesh' row (692-749, in Mongolia) is probably this khaganate under the wrong name (notes).

region.text: the Pyongyang district, which the Cliopatria 682 shape no longer has (the part of it that is not Hwanghae, Gyeonggi or Gangwon, already lost to Silla in 676)

ledger.note: c. 682: the Pyongyang district leaves the Tang map. 'Silla failed to regain the former Goguryeo territories north of the Taedong River, which were now under Tang dominion', yet the Andong seat had been 'moved to the Old City of Liaodong' in the second month of 676 and to Xincheng in 677 (Silla-Tang page, footnote): the Tang administration had left Pyongyang. No page says who held the district afterwards ('Later, most of the land north of the Taedong River went to Balhae'), so the loss is to nobody; 682 is the year Cliopatria's shape drops it (and its Unified Silla row begins), a bridge.

region.text: the Four Garrisons, from which Tang troops withdrew in 686; 'Tibet establishes control over the Western Regions' in 687

ledger.note: 687: the Tarim lost again. 'In 686 Tang troops withdrew from the Four Garrisons' after 'elements within the court argued for the decrease of military expenditures'; 'In 687 the Tibetan Empire established control over the Western Regions'.

690: Wu Zetian proclaims the Zhou. Established 17 October 690 with herself as huangdi, having deposed Ruizong; 'Historians generally regard the Wu Zhou as an interregnum of the Tang dynasty': same state, same colour (rule 2), an era caption as the reference video does.
690: the capital is Luoyang, renamed Shendu (Divine Capital).

region.text: the Western Regions, pacified by Wang Xiaojie; the Anxi Protectorate re-established at Qiuci

ledger.note: 692: Wang Xiaojie recovers the Four Garrisons. 'In 692 Tang troops under Wang Xiaojie pacified the Western Regions and established the Anxi Protectorate at Qiuci' (Anxi page); the Tibetan Empire page: 'In 692, the Tibetans lost the Tarim Basin to the Chinese'.

region.text: the Goguryeo land in Manchuria and northern Korea that the Cliopatria 692-704 shape holds and its 705 shape does not (Jilin, the Yalu basin, Pyongan), without Liaodong

ledger.note: c. 705: the Tang lose the Goguryeo heartland east of Liaodong, where Balhae rises. 'Parhae was founded in 698 by Tae Choyong', after 'three Mohe chieftains took advantage of the Khitan rebellion to move further east' in 696 (Balhae page); the Balhae dossier has the state grow to the Cliopatria 705 outline at the same time from nobody's land. No page dates the Tang withdrawal; 705 is the year Cliopatria's shape drops the land, a bridge.

705: the Tang restored. The Wu Zhou page: infobox 'Emperor Wu Zetian deposed: 21 February 705'; Zhongzong 'was restored to the throne in the Shenlong Coup in 705, marking the restoration of the Tang dynasty'. The Tang page: 'the Tang was formally restored on March 3'. The list of emperors starts Zhongzong's second reign on 23 February 705.
705: the court returns to Chang'an (infobox: Chang'an 618-690 and 705-904).

region.text: Liaodong, where the Andong protectorate sat at Xincheng (Fushun) from 677

ledger.note: 714: the Andong protectorate leaves Liaodong. 'In 677 the seat was moved to Xincheng, in modern Fushun, Liaoning' and 'In 714, the seat was moved to Pingzhou, in modern Lulong County, Qinhuangdao, Hebei' (Pacify the East page); the protectorate was 'abandoned in 756 or ended in 761'. The page never says Liaodong was lost, so the loss is a reading of the seat's move west (confidence 1); Cliopatria drops Liaodong already in 705.

region.text: Suyab (Suiye), the Anxi protectorate's seat from 670, and the Chu and Ili valleys won in 657

ledger.note: 719: the Turgesh capture Suyab. 'The protectorate's seat was moved to Suyab, known as Suiye to the Chinese' (670); 'In 719 the Turgesh captured Suiye' (Anxi page). The Turgesh page and the turgesh dossier have Wuzhile taking Suyab already in 703 and ruling 'from Chach to Turfan and Beshbaliq'; 719 is used here because the same Turgesh page has the Turgesh attacking Ting Prefecture in 735 and the Anxi page has Beiting set up at Ting Prefecture in 702 and still Chinese-commanded in 789, so Turfan and Beshbalik stayed Tang.

region.text: Nanzhao, Piluoge's united Six Zhao around Dali

ledger.note: 738: Nanzhao recognised as a Tang tributary. 'In the year 737 AD, Piluoge united the Six Zhaos in succession'; the Tang granted him 'the Chinese-style name Meng Guiyi' and a title; infobox established 738. Cliopatria's Nanzhao row begins 741.

region.text: Nanzhao, after the Tang defeat at Xiaguan

ledger.note: 751: Nanzhao breaks with the Tang. Xianyu Zhongtong's army 'was defeated by Duan Jianwei with heavy losses (many due to disease) at Xiaguan'; 'By the end of 754, Geluofeng had established an alliance with the Tibetans against the Tang that would last until 794'; the Tibetan Empire page says Nanzhao 'remained under Tibetan control from 750 to 794'.

region.text: Transoxania: 'End of Tang presence in Transoxania'

ledger.note: July 751: the Battle of Talas; the abbasid-caliphate takes the Tang's place in Transoxiana. Gao Xianzhi's army 'was defeated by the Abbasid army under Ziyad ibn Salih and Karluk mercenaries'; 'The defeat marked the end of Tang influence in Transoxiana and halted Tang westward expansion', but 'no significant loss or gain of territory occurred and the borders remained relatively unchanged', so only the influence west of the Pamirs ends; the Tarim garrisons stay. The same page records that 'Shash (Tashkent) re-established its vassal status in 753 when its ruler received titles from the Tang' and that the Tang recovered Little and Great Balur in 753; neither is modelled (no region name for them).

region.text: Fanyang (Youzhou) and Hebei, An Lushan's base

ledger.note: 755: An Lushan rebels. On 16 December 755 he 'mobilized his army and marched out of Fanyang'; he 'declared himself Emperor of the new Great Yan dynasty' on 5 February 756. The rebel state needs a dossier of type rebel (notes).

region.text: the Yellow River plain between Fanyang, Luoyang and Tongguan, where the fighting ran until 763

ledger.note: 755-763: the An Lushan rebellion's fighting zone (rule 6 blend where neither side holds firmly). Infobox dates '16 December 755 - 17 February 763'; 'the Battle of Yongqiu, in the spring of 756, went badly for An Lushan'.

region.text: the Eastern Capital, Luoyang

ledger.note: 756: Luoyang falls to the rebels. He 'captured the "Eastern Capital" city of Luoyang on 18 January 756'.

region.text: the capital Chang'an and Guanzhong, after the defeat at Tongguan on 7 July 756

ledger.note: 756: Chang'an falls. 'On 7 July, the Tang forces were defeated [at Tongguan]. The road to the capital now lay open'; 'In July 756 An Lushan and his rebel forces captured Chang'an'; after reaching Sichuan Xuanzong abdicated on 12 August and Li Heng 'was proclaimed Emperor Suzong at Lingzhou'.

region.text: both Chang'an and Luoyang

ledger.note: 757: the capitals recovered. 'With Uyghur assistance, the Tang Imperial forces recaptured both Chang'an and Luoyang in late 757'; An Lushan had been killed by his son on 29 January 757; An Qingxu 'abandoned Luoyang and fled north' to Yecheng.

region.text: Bian (Kaifeng) and Luoyang, taken by Shi Siming

ledger.note: 759: Luoyang falls again. Shi Siming kills An Qingxu on 10 April 759, is enthroned as Emperor Zhaowu of Yan and takes Bian and Luoyang (the page gives no exact date for Luoyang); the front stalemates at Heyang and Shan.

region.text: Luoyang, retaken for the second time in winter 762

ledger.note: 762: Luoyang recovered. 'in the winter of 762, the eastern capital Luoyang was retaken by Tang forces for the second time.'

region.text: Yanqi (Karashahr), conquered by the Tibetan Empire in 763

ledger.note: 763: Tibet takes Yanqi. 'In 763 the Tibetan Empire conquered Yanqi' (Protectorate General to Pacify the West page). Yanqi is Karasahr (see the 644 event: 'Karasahr was also conquered, and was known to the Chinese as Yanqi'); the 150 km circle is the one the tibetan-empire dossier uses (ledger 27, 763 gain). The rest of the Anxi and Beiting garrisons stay Tang until 787-792. [fx-11, 2026-11-01] The 763 and 768 keyframes now leave this circle out of the Tarim they add.

region.text: the rebellion's fighting zone

ledger.note: 763: the An Lushan rebellion ends. 'Shi Chaoyi killed himself rather than be captured' on 17 February 763; infobox 'Tang victory'.

region.text: Hebei, where surrendered Yan generals keep their posts as jiedushi

ledger.note: 763: Hebei returns to the Tang in name. 'In Hebei, three fanzhen became virtually independent for the remainder of the Tang dynasty' (An Lushan page): drawn as Tang for the nominal allegiance; a vassal tint would be defensible and the reviewer may ask for it.

region.text: Chang'an, occupied for fifteen days from 18 November 763

ledger.note: 763: Tibet in Chang'an. Tibetan forces 'proceeded to briefly capture Chang'an on 18 November 763'; they 'occupied Chang'an for fifteen days and installed a puppet emperor' (Tibetan Empire page). Hatched, rule 4; not a change of owner.

region.text: Chang'an

ledger.note: 763: the Tibetans leave Chang'an after fifteen days.

region.text: Liang Prefecture (Liangzhou), 'cutting off the Anxi and Beiting protectorates from the Tang dynasty'; the rest of the corridor (Ganzhou, Suzhou, Guazhou, Shazhou) over the following decades

ledger.note: 764: Tibet takes Liangzhou and cuts off the west. 'In 764 the Tibetan Empire invaded the Hexi Corridor and conquered Liang Prefecture', 'cutting off the Anxi and Beiting protectorates from the Tang dynasty' (Anxi page). The pages opened date only Liangzhou; the ledger places the whole corridor's loss here (confidence 2) and the window agent may stage it westward; a gap-filler should open 'Hexi Corridor' for the dates of Ganzhou, Suzhou, Guazhou and Shazhou.

region.text: Longyou and Hexi, fought over until the 783 treaty

ledger.note: 764-783: the Tang-Tibetan war for Longyou and Hexi after the An Lushan rebellion. The An Lushan page: after the rebellion Tibet went on 'to conquer much of the western half of Tang territories'; the Anxi page: 'In 764 the Tibetan Empire invaded the Hexi Corridor'. Tibet reached Chang'an on 18 November 763 (An Lushan page).

region.text: the Tang–Tibetan frontier as the 783 treaty 'defined the borders'

ledger.note: 783: a treaty defines the Tang-Tibetan borders. 'At this time, a 783 treaty between the Tibetan Empire and the Tang dynasty defined the borders' (the page does not name the treaty); it adds that the 821/822 treaty 'established peace for more than two decades' and 'Borders were again confirmed ... through his 821-823 treaty'. Longyou and Hexi stay Tibetan (researcher's reading of the borders the Tang page and the ledger show). The Tibetan frontier is sharp from here (certainty).

region.text: Qiuci (Kucha), seat of the Anxi protectorate

ledger.note: 787: Kucha falls. 'In 787 the Tibetan Empire conquered Qiuci.' The garrison had been cut off since 764 ('cutting off the Anxi and Beiting protectorates from the Tang dynasty'); 'In 780 Guo Xin and Li Yuanzhong were officially made protectorate generals' (Anxi page).

region.text: the Beiting protectorate north of the Tianshan and the Turpan basin: the Anxi page says 'the last vestiges of the protectorate and its garrisons were defeated by Tibetan forces by 790'

ledger.note: c. 790: the protectorates end. 'the last vestiges of the protectorate and its garrisons were defeated by Tibetan forces by 790' (Anxi page, from a sentence on the uncertain final years). The page dates Beiting's creation (702) and its isolation (764) but not its end, so 790 for Beiting itself, and Dzungaria and Turfan as its land, are the researcher's reading (confidence 1).

region.text: Yutian (Khotan)

ledger.note: 792: Khotan falls, the last garrison. 'In 792 the Tibetan Empire conquered Yutian.'

region.text: Nanzhao, which 'switched sides to the Tang' after the battle of Shenchuan

ledger.note: 794: Nanzhao returns to the Tang. 'In 794, he launched the battle of Shenchuan to break up with Tibet and switched sides to the Tang.' A tributary tint; Nanzhao's raids from 829 show how loose it was.

region.text: Nghệ An (the Tang Hoan Prefecture, today Nghệ An and Hà Tĩnh); the page names Nghệ An only

ledger.note: 803: Champa seizes Nghe An from the Tang. 'The Cham assaulted the Tang and seized Nghệ An in 803' (Champa page; the Huanghua account has Huanwang invading Annan, the Tang's southernmost province, in 803). Hà Tĩnh is the researcher's reading, as in the champa dossier.

region.text: the regions lost in 803

ledger.note: 809: the Tang recover Nghe An. 'The Chinese barely defeated the Cham and recovered lost regions in 809' (Champa page).

region.text: Shazhou (Dunhuang) and Guazhou, captured 'from the Tibetans'

ledger.note: 848: Zhang Yichao rises at Dunhuang. 'In 848, Zhang Yichao, a resident of Shazhou, led an uprising and captured Shazhou and Guazhou from the Tibetans.' Cliopatria's Tibetan Empire row ends 849 ('Tibetans' from 850); the Tibetan Empire page's infobox gives 'Disestablished: 842/848' and ascribes the collapse to the Battle of U-Yor over Langdarma's successor.

region.text: Ganzhou, Suzhou, and Yizhou

ledger.note: 850: the corridor recovered. 'By 850 Zhang had captured Ganzhou, Suzhou, and Yizhou.' Suzhou (Jiuquan) is given as a coordinate because the gazetteer has no place entry for it.

region.text: Xizhou (Gaochang)

ledger.note: 851: 'In 851 Zhang captured Xizhou (Gaochang).'

region.text: Zhang's territory, named Guiyi Prefecture by the Tang court, 'usually de facto independent but nominally subordinate'

ledger.note: 851: the Guiyi Circuit. The Tang court names Zhang's territory Guiyi Prefecture and makes him Guiyi jiedushi; the Tang 'managed to restore indirect control over former territories as far west as the Hexi Corridor' (Tang page). Vassal tint over the 848-851 gains, with its own outline and label (rule 4); it outlives the Tang (to 1036).

region.text: Liangzhou, with Lanzhou, Hezhou and Kuozhou

ledger.note: 861: Guiyi's authority extends to Liangzhou 'and several other prefectures, including Lanzhou, Hezhou, and Kuozhou'. Vassal land like the rest of the circuit.

region.text: Annan (Songping and Junzhou), occupied 'for three years'

ledger.note: 863: Nanzhao takes Annam. 'Shilong attacked Annan again in 863, occupying it for three years.'

region.text: Annan, retaken by Gao Pian

ledger.note: 866: Annam recovered. 'Gao completed the retaking of Annan in fall 866.'

region.text: Xizhou (Gaochang)

ledger.note: 866: Xizhou (Gaochang) is lost to the Uyghurs of Qocho. The Guiyi page: 'In 851 Zhang captured Xizhou (Gaochang)'; its 866 entry: 'Xizhou was also captured by the Uyghurs' (after 'they were immediately captured by the Kingdom of Qocho afterwards'). The page does not give the month.

region.text: Yizhou (Hami)

ledger.note: 876: Yizhou (Hami) is lost. 'In 876 the Kingdom of Qocho seized Yizhou' (timeline); Rong Xinjiang, quoted on the same page: 'in 876 the Xizhou Uighurs seized Yizhou and with this the Guiyijun lost one of its important garrisons'. Yizhou is the gazetteer place Hami (alt name Yizhou).

region.text: the Tang palace in Chang'an and Guanzhong

ledger.note: 881: Huang Chao takes Chang'an. 'In 881, Huang Chao moved into the Tang palace in Chang'an and declared himself the emperor of a new state of Qi' (reign from 16 January 881); 'forcing Emperor Xizong to flee'. The rebel state needs a dossier of type rebel (notes).

region.text: Chang'an, which Huang Chao 'abandoned' when Li Keyong entered it in summer 883

ledger.note: 883: Chang'an retaken. 'In summer 883, Li Keyong entered Chang'an, and Huang was unable to resist him, and so abandoned Chang'an to flee east'; Huang Chao killed on 13 July 884; the rebellion 'permanently destroyed the power of the Tang dynasty'.

region.text: Nanzhao, Piluoge's united Six Zhao around Dali

ledger.note: 902: Nanzhao ends. 'In 902, the dynasty came to a bloody end when the chief minister (buxie), Zheng Maisi, murdered the royal family' (infobox: overthrown 902). Nanzhao's attacks on the Tang run 829-877 on the same page, so the tributary tint of 794 is nominal.
904: the court moved to Luoyang. Zhu Wen, who 'seized control of the Tang capital Chang'an' in 901, forces the move in 903-904 and has Zhaozong killed (22 September 904); infobox: Luoyang 904-907.

region.text: Yizhou (Hami) and Xizhou (Gaochang)

ledger.note: 904: Zhang Chengfeng retakes Yizhou and Xizhou. 'In 904, Zhang Chengfeng attacked Qocho and seized Yizhou (Hami) and Xizhou (Gaochang).' The land is part of the Guiyi Circuit, a Tang vassal.

region.text: the Tang's remaining territory: 'most of northern China' to the Later Liang, while the regional governors keep Sichuan, the Yangtze, Zhejiang, Fujian, Lingnan, Hunan, Shanxi, western Shaanxi and northern Hebei as the Ten Kingdoms, Jin, Qi and Yan

ledger.note: 907: Zhu Wen ends the Tang. 'In 907, the Tang dynasty was ended when Zhu deposed Ai and took the throne for himself'; infobox 'Abdication in favour of Later Liang: June 1, 907' (the emperor list gives Ai's deposition as 12 May 907). Successors and their land in identity.successors; Cliopatria's four extra years (to 910) go to them.

region.text: the Guiyi Circuit, 'usually de facto independent but nominally subordinate to the Tang dynasty'

ledger.note: 907: the Tang ends and the Guiyi Circuit carries on alone. 'In 910 Zhang Chengfeng received news of the Tang dynasty's demise and declared himself Emperor Baiyi'; 'In 1036 the Tanguts ... annexed the Kingdom of Guiyi'.

wars.name: Tang campaign against the Eastern Turks

zones.text: the Ordos and the steppe south of the Gobi

wars.outcome: Tang victory: Illig Qaghan captured in 630 and the khaganate overthrown; the Ashina settled in the Ordos Loop as vassals (buffer state 639-645, reconquered 645).
wars.note: The Eastern Turkic page: 'In 627-629, an unusual cold led to mass livestock deaths and famine' and 'Six Tang armies attacked on a 1,200 km (750 mi) front' in 629; the war's years here are the page's capture year (630), since 629 is the page's rebellion year.

wars.name: Tang campaigns against the Western Turks
wars.outcome: Tang victory; fall of the Western Turkic Khaganate in 657 and the Tang's largest extent. The page's own span is 640-712 (the last Western Turkic remnants absorbed by the Second Turkic Khaganate in 712).

wars.name: Goguryeo–Tang War and the fall of Baekje
wars.outcome: Baekje toppled in 660 by a Tang-Silla invasion (Tang page) and Goguryeo destroyed by 668; the Protectorate General to Pacify the East was set up and 'based in Pyongyang'.
wars.note: The pages opened do not date the start of the Goguryeo-Tang War itself; 660 is the first dated step. Contested-zone shading only for the years the Silla-Tang page dates (see the Silla-Tang War entry).

wars.name: Silla–Tang War

zones.text: the peninsula south of the Taedong River

wars.outcome: Silla victory: Silla controls the Korean peninsula south of the Taedong River (Baekje from 671, the rest in 676), the Tang keep Liaodong and the Goguryeo land north of it; the Andong seat retreats to Liaoyang (676) and Xincheng (677); the page records a formal Tang recognition of Silla's sovereignty south of the Taedong in 736.

wars.name: Tang–Tibetan war for the Four Garrisons
wars.outcome: Tibet takes Qiuci and the Tarim in 670 (Dafei River), the Tang retake it in 673, Tibet in 677, the Tang again in 679, the Tang withdraw in 686 and Tibet establishes control in 687; Wang Xiaojie recovers it for the Tang in 692 and the Anxi Protectorate is re-established at Qiuci.
wars.note: The Anxi page: 670 Tibet; 673 Tang; 677 Tibet; 679 Tang; 686 Tang withdrawal; 687 Tibet; 692 Tang. The Western Turks page adds that a Western Turkic tribe allied with the Tibetan Empire invaded the Tarim Basin in 670 and in 677. The swings are in the ledger as loss/gain.

wars.name: Tang–Nanzhao war

zones.text: Xiaguan (751) and the approaches to Dali

wars.outcome: Tang defeated at Xiaguan in 751; Li Mi's 754 army 'never made it past Mu'ege'; Nanzhao allied with Tibet from 754 to 794.
wars.note: No ground changed hands, so the ledger carries only the vassal_end of 751.

wars.name: Battle of Talas
wars.outcome: Abbasid victory in July 751; 'Consolidation of Abbasid rule in Transoxania; End of Tang presence in Transoxania', but 'no significant loss or gain of territory occurred and the borders remained relatively unchanged'; the Tang recovered Little and Great Balur in 753 (page).
wars.note: Empty zones: no cell changes owner; the ledger ends the Transoxiana vassal tint.

wars.name: An Lushan rebellion

zones.text: Luoyang, Bian, the Heyang and Shan fronts

wars.outcome: Tang victory on 17 February 763 (Shi Chaoyi's suicide), with Uyghur assistance in the recapture of Chang'an and Luoyang in late 757; the Western Regions lost 'most of its control' to troop withdrawal, and 'three fanzhen became virtually independent' in Hebei.
wars.note: Rebel-held land is the Yan rebel state's (rule 5), the fighting zone between Luoyang and Tongguan the blend (rule 6). Infobox dates 16 December 755 to 17 February 763.

wars.name: Tang–Tibetan war after the An Lushan rebellion

zones.text: Liangzhou 764, then the corridor to Dunhuang
Chang'an, occupied fifteen days in November 763

wars.outcome: Tibet captured Chang'an for fifteen days in November 763, took Liang Prefecture in 764 and cut off the Anxi and Beiting protectorates; a 783 treaty defined the borders; the garrisons fall in 787-792 (Anxi page).

wars.name: Nanzhao's campaigns against the Tang

zones.text: Chengdu, attacked 829, besieged 869, approached within 70 km in 873-874: no ground held

wars.outcome: Annam lost in 863 and retaken by Gao Pian in fall 866; the Sichuan campaigns held no ground; Shilong's death in 877 'effectively ended Nanzhao's expansionist campaigns'.
wars.note: The Chengdu zone is listed so the reviewer sees it was considered; only Annam enters the ledger.

wars.name: Huang Chao rebellion
wars.outcome: Chang'an retaken by Li Keyong in summer 883; Huang Chao killed on 13 July 884; the rebellion 'permanently destroyed the power of the Tang dynasty'.
wars.note: A roving army until 881 (Huang Chao page: Guangzhou conquered, undated; Chang'an captured 'In 881'), so no southern zone is shaded; the page gives 874-884 as the rebellion's span.

wars.name: Transition from Sui to Tang (Tang unification wars)

zones.text: Dou Jiande's Xia and Liu Heita, 621-623

wars.outcome: Tang victory over every rival: Qin (618), Liang of Hexi (619), Dingyang (620), Xia and Zheng at Hulao (621), Liang of Xiao Xian (621), Wu (621), Liu Heita (623), Song (624), Gao Kaidao's Yan (624), Liang Shidu (628). 'The transition ended in 628.'
wars.note: Rival states listed under counterparts_needing_dossiers in the report; the pages give years for most and places for few.

certainty.note: The steppe, Tarim and Tibetan frontiers are approximate; the provincial frontiers in the south follow Tang circuits; the Korean frontier is the Taedong River from 676 (Silla-Tang page).
The Tibetan frontier is sharp from the 783 treaty that 'defined the borders' (Tibetan Empire page) and the 821/822 treaty until the Tibetan collapse of 842-848; every other frontier stays soft.

Re-opened in the repair: seat of Andong moved to the Old City of Liaodong in the second month of 676 and to Xincheng in 677; Tang held the land north of the Taedong; 'Later, most of the land north of the Taedong River went to Balhae' (no year).

sources.title: Lin Shihong
sources.note: Review repair: Lin 'controlled most of modern Jiangxi and Guangdong'; offered to surrender in winter 622 and 'died in 622, and his followers scattered, ending his state of Chu'; successor Emperor Gaozu of Tang.

sources.title: Xueyantuo
sources.note: Review repair: 'On August 1, 646, the Xueyantuo were defeated by the Uyghurs (Huihe) and the Tang'; the khaganate 'spanned from the Altai Mountains to the Gobi Desert'; says nothing of the Yanran protectorate.

sources.title: Protectorate General to Pacify the East
sources.note: Review repair: Andong created at Pyongyang in 668; seat to Liaoyang by 676, to Xincheng (Fushun) in 677, to Pingzhou (Lulong, Hebei) in 714, to Liaoxi in 743; 'abandoned in 756 or ended in 761'; no date for the loss of Pyongyang, Liaodong or Manchuria and no mention of Balhae.

sources.title: Balhae
sources.note: Review repair: founded in 698 by Tae Choyong; the Khitan rebellion of 696; Tang title 713 or 714; no date for the end of Tang control of Liaodong or the Goguryeo land and no Taedong boundary before 736 (not stated).

sources.title: Champa
sources.note: Review repair: 'The Cham assaulted the Tang and seized Nghe An in 803'; 'recovered lost regions in 809'; Hoan, Ai and Ha Tinh not named.

sources.title: Turgesh
sources.note: Review repair: 'In 703 he captured Suyab and set up his authority on the territory from Chach to Turfan and Beshbaliq'; Turgesh attack Ting Prefecture in 735; no 719 and no Tang control of Suyab stated (conflicts with the Anxi page's 719).

sources.title: Beiting Protectorate
sources.note: Review repair: opened to date the protectorate's end; the page is a list of Astana Graves captions and states no founding, jurisdiction or end (stub).

sources.title: Emperor Gaozu of Tang
sources.note: Opened by fx-11 (1 Nov 2026) for the 623 snap: 'Li Xiaogong was able to persuade the Sui cities in modern southern Shaanxi, Sichuan, and Chongqing to submit' (paragraph on the winter-617 capture of Chang'an); Du Fuwei 'who controlled the modern southern Anhui, submitted to Tang' (summer 619); Xu Yuanlang 'rose in revolt, occupying the modern Shandong region' (621).

sources.title: Li Xiaogong
sources.note: Opened by fx-11: Li Yuan 'made Li Xiaogong in charge of a campaign to persuade or capture the region south of the Qinling Mountains'; 'Li Xiaogong was able to persuade some 30 commanderies to submit to Li Yuan' (no month or year on the page).

sources.title: Du Fuwei
sources.note: Opened by fx-11: his state was the land south of the Huai River, first based at Liyang (Chaohu, Anhui), from 620 at Danyang (Nanjing); he decided to submit in 619; 'In summer 620 ... Prince of Wu'; died April 624.

sources.title: Xu Shiji
sources.note: Opened by fx-11: Xu Yuanlang, Prince of Lu, controlled central and western Shandong and was Liu Heita's ally; by spring 623 he abandoned his capital at Yan Prefecture and was killed in flight.

sources.title: Yenisei Kyrgyz
sources.note: Opened by fx-11: homeland 'the southern portion of the Minusinsk Hollow'; 'The heart of their homeland was the forested Tannu-Ola mountain range' in modern Tuva; silent on any Tang rule over the Kyrgyz in 630-680 (the Tang link it describes is Zhongzong's letter in the early 8th century).

sources.title: Western Turkic Khaganate
sources.note: fx-35: infobox 'Vassal of the Tang dynasty (657–742)', Kunling Protectorate 657–736, Mengchi Protectorate 657–742; claimants Mishe 657–662, Buzhen 657–667, Duzhi 676–679, Yuanqing 685–692; 'several puppet khagans'.

notes:
Written by the ea-04-a research agent on 2026-10-19 from the Phase A worked example (polities/_example-tang-dynasty.json, kept unchanged), re-checked against the pages listed in sources[] (all opened in this run, accessed 2026-10-19). 17 pages: 15 for the Tang plus the Transition from Sui to Tang and Gao Kaidao pages, which were opened for the gao-kaidao dossier and shared (budget for the Tang was 14).

Changes against the example: (1) the 783 treaty and the 764-783 contest now cite the Tibetan Empire and An Lushan pages, because the Tang page does not mention a 783 treaty (it gives the 821 Changqing treaty); the treaty's name (Qingshui) was dropped because no page opened names it. (2) The Sui-Tang transition is filled from the Transition page: events 618-628 for Qin, Liang of Hexi, Dingyang, Zheng, Xia, Liang (Xiao Xian), Wu, Handong (Liu Heita), Song and Gao Kaidao's Yan, plus the 623 keyframe correction (Cliopatria's 623-625 shape misses the Yangtze). (3) The Tarim swings 673 and 677 are added from the Anxi page. (4) Baekje is lost in 671 and the rest of southern Korea in 676 (Silla-Tang page); the example had both in 676. (5) Xizhou (866) and Yizhou (876) leave the Guiyi land; Zhang Chengfeng retakes both in 904 (Guiyi page). (6) The Wu Zetian-era ruler and the emperor reigns are checked against the emperor list. (7) Claims and quotes that none of the pages opened carries were removed: the Tang-Uyghur alliance of 788-789, 'By 790 Chinese control over the Tarim Basin was completely lost', the usual-accounts 781-787 for Hexi, the Abbasid mercenaries at An Lushan, Khotan and Kashgar submitting in 632, Guo Xin holding office to 808, Yongqiu having 'prevented the Yan forces from conquering southern China', Uyghur help sought in 756, the Uyghurs possibly taking Dzungaria, and the Hebei fanzhen being called Tang jiedushi 'by the sources'. (8) The Tang-Nanzhao and Guiyi vassal tints now end (Nanzhao 902, Guiyi 907).

Pages not re-opened (so claims that rested on them were rewritten or dropped): Protectorate General to Pacify the East, Beiting Protectorate (a stub), Later Liang (Five Dynasties), Anxi Protectorate (a redirect). The 668 event now cites the Silla-Tang page; the 907 event the Tang page.

Disagreements between pages: Tuyuhun's fall 663 (Tibetan Empire page) or 670 (Tuyuhun infobox); Ai's deposition 12 May 907 (emperor list) or the abdication of 1 June 907 (Tang page, infobox); Wu Zetian's proclamation 16 October 690 (Tang page) or 17 October (Wu Zhou page, infobox) -- the ledger uses 17 October; the Western Turks page lists Kucha's campaign as 648 in its lead and the surrender as 19 January 649; Huang Chao's death 13 July 884 at Langhu Valley by his nephew's hand (some accounts say suicide); Yizhou's captor in 876 (Kingdom of Qocho, or the Xizhou Uighurs); Nanzhao's break with the Tang 750 (Tibetan Empire page: 'under Tibetan control from 750 to 794'), 751 (Xiaguan) or 754 (alliance with Tibet).

Cliopatria rows and relations: the Tang begins 623 instead of 618 and ends 910 instead of 907 (successors start 911); the Sui row runs to 627 (rival remnants); Gao Kaidao 623-625 ends in 624 (own dossier); the Mongolian Plateau is drawn as direct Tang territory 633-681 (Xueyantuo until 645; the Anbei page: Tang controlled the Mongolian Plateau 647-682, jimi-style, as a vassal tint); the 661-673 shapes reach Khorasan; Hexi and the Western Regions are removed in 757 although Liangzhou fell in 764 and Kucha in 787; the Guiyi Circuit's Hexi (848-907) is given to 'Tibetans' and 'Ganzhou Kingdom'. The 'Turgesh' 692-749 (Mongolia) and 'Turks' 666-756 (Kazakhstan/Kyrgyzstan) labels look swapped (Inner Asia group).

States Cliopatria lacks that this dossier's counterparts need: Yan (An Lushan, 755-763; slug yan-an-lushan, type rebel: Hebei, Luoyang 756-757 and 759-762, Chang'an 756-757); Qi (Huang Chao, 881-883; slug qi-huang-chao, type rebel: Guanzhong); the Guiyi Circuit (848-1036); three Sui-Tang warlord states with no dossier yet: Li Gui's Liang of Hexi (surrendered c. 619), Liu Heita's Handong (622-623) and Fu Gongshi's Song (623-624). The other warlord counterparts, the Xueyantuo, Gaochang and Kucha already have dossiers (xue-ju-s-qin, liu-wuzhou-s-dingyang, wang-shichong-s-zheng, dou-jiande-s-xia, xiao-xian-s-liang, li-zitong-s-wu, lin-shihong-s-chu, liang-shidu-s-liang, kingdom-of-gaochang, kingdom-of-kucha) and the ledger uses their slugs. The Yanran/Anbei, Anxi, Beiting and Andong protectorates are not states: they are the vassal tint over the regions the ledger names. Not modelled for lack of a region name or a date: Tashkent's vassal status (re-established 753), Gilgit/Balur (747, 753), Du Fuwei's submission (c. 619, Prince of Wu), the Tuyuhun campaigns of 635-636.

Cross-checks with sister dossiers (read only for dates, not opened as pages): their mirror events differ from this ledger where the Transition page is thinner. liu-wuzhou-s-dingyang records a 619 capture of Taiyuan from the Tang, dou-jiande-s-xia a 619 capture of Liyang and liang-shidu-s-liang a 622 loss of the eastern city of Shuofang; none of the pages opened here gives those, so the Tang ledger has no matching loss (a gap-filler can add them). li-zitong-s-wu has Jiangdu abandoned in 620 and the Wu surrendering at Hangzhou in winter 621 with Zhejiang as its land, where the Transition page names only Jiangdu: this ledger keeps the page's 621 and the Yangzhou radius, and the 623 keyframe correction adds only that and the Jiangling area, so the real southern extent in 621-625 is wider (xiao-xian-s-liang gives Hubei, Hunan, Guangxi and Tonkin; the Tang 626 shape contains them). xue-ju-s-qin dates the Qin's end to December 618 (this ledger: 618, no month). lin-shihong-s-chu dates the Chu's end to 622 and names Jiangxi and Guangdong, which the ledger follows at confidence 1.

Region names used that the gazetteer may lack: none (Yizhou is the gazetteer's Hami; Suzhou (Jiuquan) is still a coordinate). The Tang area comparison: infobox 5.4 M km2 for 715, Cliopatria 4.03 M km2 for 705-749 (ratio 0.75, within the factor-of-two check); the 661-665 shape (8.73 M km2) is 1.6 times the infobox figure and reaches Khorasan, marked adjust; the Tibetan Empire page gives 4.6 M km2 for 800 (Cliopatria's Tibetan shapes should be compared by that group).
